findings.claim: 25 questions worded 'Explain two consequences of...' are labelled '4 marks - Consequence Question' with band ladders topping at [4]. The error runs through all 12 lessons and is repeated in three exam tips (L2, L6, L9); L2's exam tip also states 'The mark scheme awards each consequence separately out of two marks.'
findings.truth: On the Edexcel period study the consequence question is worth 8 marks, 4 for each of the two consequences. The spec's assessment section gives booklet P 32 marks over four questions: Q1(a) and 1(b) on consequence, Q2 an 8-mark analytical narrative, and Q3 two importance parts of 8 marks each (4+4+8+16 = 32). The unit already contradicts itself: L9's exam tip correctly says 'Each consequence is marked separately out of 4'. A student practising to a 4-mark ceiling writes half the required development.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, 'Paper 2: Period study and British depth study' assessment section (booklet P, 32 marks, Q1(a)/1(b) consequence, Q2 analytical narrative, Q3 two of three importance parts)

findings.claim: Fourteen invented exam citations across nine lessons: 'sometimes loosely called the 1945 Zionist conference in exam mark schemes' and 'Examiner mark schemes ... explicitly reward pre-1948 material' (L1); 'Examiner indicative content for the ... question rewards balanced perspectives' (L2); 'A summer 2024 Q2 narrative asked specifically about ...' and '(a real Q2 from summer 2023)' (L4); 'Indicative content for importance of the Suez Crisis ... rewards' (L5); 'Indicative content for the closure of the Straits expects' (L6); 'The 2022 Q3 examiner exemplar shows' and 'is the actual 2022 Q3 prompt' (L8); 'The 2024 indicative content rewards' (L9); 'Examiner indicative content for the 2023 importance prompt' and 'is a real 2023 question' (L10); 'supported by examiner indicative content' and 'The 2023 importance prompt asked specifically about ... Examiner mark schemes reward' (L11).
findings.truth: No such papers, examiner reports, exemplars or indicative content exist to cite, and 'indicative content' is board mark-scheme vocabulary the house rules keep out of lesson text. The advice attached to each citation is sound and is kept; only the invented authority is removed.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md (the only exam authority available); scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT_HISTORY.md copyright-distancing rule

findings.claim: Fifteen further 'examiners reward' / 'examiners want' / 'mark schemes reward' assertions and three collapsible headings framed round examiner behaviour ('Why the King David Hotel bombing matters in mark schemes', 'How examiners reward Suez analysis on the Q3 importance prompt', 'How examiners reward Q1 consequence answers on the Straits of Tiran', 'Why territories vs the territories matters for examiners').
findings.truth: Claims about what examiners reward are not in the specification and cannot be verified. Each is reworded into the house voice ('the question asks for', 'a strong answer') without losing the guidance.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/CHECK_PROMPT_HISTORY.md; specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md carries no statement about what examiners reward

findings.claim: 'Specific consequences include: the immediate British round-up of around 2,700 Jewish suspects (Operation Agatha and follow-up sweeps)' - given as a consequence of the King David Hotel bombing of 22 July 1946, and repeated in the mark scheme for practice question 2.
findings.truth: Cause and effect are reversed. Operation Agatha ran from 29 June to 1 July 1946 and detained about 2,700 people; the Irgun bombed the King David Hotel in retaliation for it. The British response to the bombing was Operation Shark, 30 July to 2 August 1946, which screened about 102,000 people in Tel Aviv and detained between 500 and 787.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Operation Agatha' (29 June - 1 July 1946, c.2,700 detained, Irgun retaliated by bombing the King David Hotel); Wikipedia 'Operation Shark' (30 July - 2 August 1946, c.102,000 screened, 500-787 arrested)

findings.claim: UNSCOP's 'report, published in August, contained two plans'.
findings.truth: The UNSCOP report is dated 3 September 1947.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'United Nations Special Committee on Palestine' (report dated 3 September 1947; eleven member countries)

findings.claim: 'Israeli casualties were roughly 800 dead and 2,500 wounded; Arab casualties were perhaps 18,000 to 20,000 dead' (repeated in flashcard 14).
findings.truth: Israeli wounded numbered about 4,517, not 2,500. Arab dead are estimated at 9,800-15,000 Egyptians killed or missing, 1,000-2,500 Syrians and about 700 Jordanians, so 18,000-20,000 overstates the top of the range.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Six-Day War' infobox (Israel 776-983 killed, 4,517 wounded; Egypt 9,800-15,000; Syria 1,000-2,500; Jordan 696-700)

findings.claim: The PFLP 'hijacked four civil airliners on the same day, flew three of them to a desert strip in Jordan ... and held more than 300 hostages for ten days', and the key fact says the hijackings 'took four civil airliners to Dawson's Field'.
findings.truth: Four hijackings were attempted on 6 September 1970 and three succeeded (the El Al attempt was foiled). Only TWA 741 and Swissair 100 reached Dawson's Field that day; Pan Am 93 was flown to Cairo. BOAC 775 was hijacked on 9 September and taken to Dawson's Field, making three aircraft there. There were 310 hostages and most were freed on 11 September; the aircraft were destroyed on 12 September.

findings.claim: 'By 22 October Israel had pushed back, encircled the Egyptian Third Army on the west bank of the Canal'.
findings.truth: The Egyptian Third Army was on the east bank of the Suez Canal, in Sinai. Israeli forces crossed westward in Operation Gazelle from 15 October and cut the Third Army's supply lines from the west bank; the encirclement closed after the failed 22 October ceasefire.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Yom Kippur War' (Operation Gazelle, 15 October crossing; 'Egypt's trapped Third Army' east of the canal; second ceasefire 25 October)

findings.claim: 'From 1968 Israeli governments authorised the first Jewish settlements in the West Bank (Kfar Etzion) and Golan'.
findings.truth: Kfar Etzion, the first West Bank settlement, was re-established in 1967, and settlement policy was encouraged by the Labor government from September 1967.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Israeli settlement' ('The first settlement was Kfar Etzion, in the southern West Bank'; 'As early as September 1967, Israeli settlement policy was progressively encouraged by the Labor government'); Wikipedia 'Kfar Etzion' (cabinet decided to re-establish it in 1967)

findings.claim: 'On 26 October 1994 King Hussein and Rabin signed the Israel-Jordan peace treaty'.
findings.truth: The treaty was signed by the two prime ministers, Yitzhak Rabin for Israel and Abdelsalam al-Majali for Jordan. King Hussein, President Ezer Weizman and President Clinton attended; Clinton witnessed it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Israel-Jordan peace treaty' (signatories PM Rabin and PM Abdelsalam al-Majali; Clinton observed, Weizman and King Hussein present)

findings.claim: Mark scheme for the Gaza raid question: the deaths 'humiliated Nasser at the start of his presidency'.
findings.truth: In February 1955 Nasser was Prime Minister of Egypt. He became President in June 1956. The lesson's own glossary dates his presidency 1956-70.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the L5 glossary entry 'Gamal Abdel Nasser: President of Egypt 1956-70'

findings.truth: The content validator caps lesson descriptions under 100 characters. Shortened to 96.

findings.claim: 'From January to July 1949 Israel signed separate armistice agreements'.
findings.truth: Talks opened at Rhodes in January 1949, but the first armistice, with Egypt, was signed on 24 February 1949. The signing period ran February to July.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the 1949 Armistice Agreements (Egypt 24 February, Lebanon 23 March, Jordan 3 April, Syria 20 July 1949)

findings.claim: The Suez Canal is defined as 'The 100-mile waterway connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, opened in 1869' (same wording in the content data-def).
findings.truth: The canal is about 120 miles (193 km) today; it was roughly 102 miles when it opened in 1869, so the figure is defensible for 1869 but not for the canal now. Not corrected, because the definition is anchored to the 1869 opening.
findings.evidence: canal length 193 km today, c.164 km at opening

findings.claim: Key fact: the Haganah was 'around 60,000 strong' in 1945.
findings.truth: British post-war estimates gave the Haganah a paper strength of 75,000 and an effective strength of 30,000; another estimate puts membership at 7 per cent of the Jewish population in October 1947. 60,000 sits inside the spread but no source pins it, so it is not corrected.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Haganah' (British estimate: paper strength 75,000, effective strength 30,000)

findings.claim: 'Three Egyptian ministers resigned in protest' at Sadat's November 1977 visit to Israel.
findings.truth: Foreign Minister Ismail Fahmy and Minister of State Muhammad Riad resigned over the visit; a third resignation (Ibrahim Kamel) came later, at Camp David in 1978. The figure of three could not be verified for November 1977, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: not settled by a fetched source

findings.claim: Tunis is 'more than 1,500 miles' from Palestinian territory (L10 content and exam tip, L11 content).
findings.truth: The straight-line distance from Tunis to Jerusalem is about 1,400 miles, so 'more than 1,500' is slightly overstated. Too small to be worth three edits.

findings.claim: Three flashcards ask for a set rather than one idea: 'Name three forms of protest used in the First Intifada' (L11), 'What three things did Arafat accept in the Geneva speech?' (L11) and 'Name the four Occupied Territories Israel held by 11 June 1967' (L7).
findings.truth: The validator's enumeration test only fires on answers of 12 words or fewer that match a ', X and Y' pattern, so all three pass. They are legitimate set-recall cards and the facts are right, so they are left unchanged rather than rewritten for style.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py FC_ENUM_PATTERN; validator run over all 12 lessons returned no flashcard violations

findings.claim: Practice question 3 sets an analytical narrative on 'the deepening of conflict in Palestine in the years 1936-45', wholly before the option's 1945 start.
findings.truth: The first spec bullet, 'Conflicting interests and demands of Jews and Arabs within the British Mandate', carries no dates, so the content is in scope as background. A real narrative question would sit inside 1945-95. Kept as a background drill rather than rewritten, because the mark scheme would have to be rebuilt around a different period.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Option P5 Key topic 1 bullet 1

summary: All 12 lessons checked. 19 findings: 3 HIGH, 8 MEDIUM, 8 LOW; 13 FIX, 0 ADJUDICATE, 6 NOTE; 95 edits. No lesson is clean, because two systematic errors run through the unit: all 25 'Explain two consequences of...' questions are tariffed at 4 marks when the Edexcel period study sets 8, 4 per consequence (F1), and fourteen fabricated past-paper, examiner-exemplar and indicative-content citations prop up otherwise sound advice (F2), with fifteen more 'examiners reward' assertions behind them (F3). The worst single factual errors are the causal inversion that makes Operation Agatha a consequence of the King David Hotel bombing it actually provoked (F4), the Six Day War casualty figures (F6), the Dawson's Field hijack count (F7), the Egyptian Third Army placed on the wrong bank of the Suez Canal (F8) and King Hussein credited with signing the 1994 Jordan treaty (F10). The narrative history is otherwise accurate: the Balfour, Mandate, Resolution 181, 1948-49 war, Suez, 1967, 1973, Camp David, Lebanon, Intifada and Oslo chronologies, the Nakba and refugee figures, and the Arafat and Rabin quotations all check out.
